title: Traversing Arrays
summary: Iterate through every element in an array using the traditional index-based for loop and reverse traversal patterns.
learningOutcomes: Write bug-free for loops to traverse arrays from start to end
Modify array elements in-place during traversal
Traverse arrays in reverse order safely

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Traversing Arrays

breakdown.whatIsIt: Comprehensive exploration of Traversing Arrays in Java.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Arrays provide high-performance, contiguous in-memory storage essential for real-world software engineering.
howItWorks: Evaluates loop condition i < arr.length on each cycle.
Accesses element at index i in O(1) time.
Increments i to advance to the next contiguous memory slot.
keyTakeaways: Standard for loop header: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++).
Writing <= arr.length is an off-by-one bug that crashes with an exception.
Elements can be updated in-place via arr[i] = newValue.
Reverse traversal starts at arr.length - 1 and ends at 0 inclusive.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Forward, Reverse & In-Place Traversal
activities.description: Observe forward traversal, in-place element mutation (adding 1), and reverse iteration.

steps.explanation: Forward loop: i starts at 0, continues while i < numbers.length (4), increments by 1.
In-place modification: adds 1 to each element (6, 11, 16, 21).
Reverse loop: starts at i = numbers.length - 1 (3), decrements down to i = 0.

questions.prompt: What is the standard loop condition used to traverse an array from start to finish?
questions.explanation: The standard loop runs from 0 up to (but not including) arr.length: i = 0; i < arr.length; i++.

questions.prompt: What error occurs if a loop header is written as 'for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)'?
options: It runs in an infinite loop
On the final iteration when i == arr.length, accessing arr[i] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
questions.explanation: The condition i <= arr.length causes the loop to attempt accessing index arr.length, which throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.prompt: How do you set up a loop to traverse an array in reverse order?
questions.explanation: Reverse traversal must start at index arr.length - 1 and decrement down to index 0 inclusive: i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--.

questions.prompt: Given: 'int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] *= 2;'. What are the elements of 'a' afterwards?
questions.explanation: Each element is multiplied by 2 in-place, transforming {1, 2, 3} into {2, 4, 6}.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of 'for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)' execute if arr is 'new int[0]'?
questions.explanation: When arr.length is 0, the initial condition 0 < 0 is immediately false, so the loop body executes 0 times safely.

questions.prompt: Can you traverse only even indices using a standard for loop?
options: No, loops must always increment by 1
Yes, by updating with i += 2 instead of i++
Only by using two nested loops
Only if the array contains even numbers
questions.explanation: Using i += 2 in the loop update step visits indices 0, 2, 4, etc.

questions.prompt: What is printed by: 'int[] b = {4, 7, 2}; for (int i = b.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) System.out.print(b[i] + " ");'?
Why is the loop condition 'i < arr.length' preferred over hardcoding a number like 'i < 5'?
options: Because arr.length automatically adapts if the array size changes, preventing out-of-bounds bugs and code duplication
Because hardcoding numbers is a compile error in Java
Because arr.length makes the loop run 2x faster
Because hardcoded numbers only work for double arrays
questions.explanation: Referencing arr.length dynamically ties loop bounds to the actual array capacity, preventing maintenance bugs if the size changes.

interviewQA.question: Why is the loop condition in array traversal written as 'i < arr.length' instead of 'i <= arr.length'?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because Java arrays are 0-indexed, the last valid index is arr.length - 1. Writing 'i <= arr.length' allows 'i' to equal arr.length on the final iteration, causing 'arr[arr.length]' to throw an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: What is the time complexity of traversing an array of size N using a for loop?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The time complexity is $O(N)$ linear time because the loop visits each of the N elements exactly once. Space complexity is $O(1)$ auxiliary memory since only an integer index variable is allocated.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: How do you safely inspect adjacent elements (arr[i] and arr[i + 1]) without an out-of-bounds error?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You must adjust the loop boundary so that the index never exceeds valid bounds: write the loop condition as 'i < arr.length - 1'. When i is at arr.length - 2, i + 1 accesses arr.length - 1 (the last valid index), avoiding an exception.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: Can an array's contents be modified while traversing it with a standard for loop?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. With a standard index-based for loop, you can reassign any element directly using its index: 'arr[i] = newValue;'.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you modify the loop counter variable 'i' inside the loop body?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Modifying 'i' inside the loop body disrupts regular sequential stepping. For example, 'i++' inside the body causes elements to be skipped, while decrementing 'i' can create an infinite loop. It is considered an anti-pattern unless implementing custom parsing algorithms.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: How does array traversal benefit from CPU cache prefetching?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because arrays are stored contiguously in physical RAM, sequential traversal exhibits spatial locality. When the CPU loads arr[0] into its L1 cache line (typically 64 bytes), adjacent elements (arr[1], arr[2], etc.) are loaded into cache simultaneously, resulting in near-instant cache hits for subsequent iterations.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

interviewQA.question: How would you traverse an array backwards and why is it useful?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You traverse backwards using: 'for (int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)'. This is useful for reversing sequences, evaluating postfix expressions, processing stacks, or finding the last occurrence of a target item.
keyPoints: Emphasize memory layout, time complexity, and edge cases.

activities.title: Self-Mastery Checklist
checklist: Standard Traversal: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) visits every element sequentially.
Strict Inequality: Always use i < arr.length to prevent off-by-one ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
In-Place Modification: Standard loops allow direct element mutation via arr[i] = val.
Reverse Traversal: for (int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) counts down from the last valid index to 0.
Adjacent Element Guard: When accessing arr[i+1], stop the loop at i < arr.length - 1.
